input.question: The Hubble Deep Field shoes thousands of galaxies from soon after the Big Bang. How is it we see these galaxies in every direction of the sky if the universe has expanded so much? Shouldn't they all be centred near one place in the sky? (i.e. near the Big Bang)
input.ground_truth: The Big Bang was not an event which happened in a particular location. It happened everywhere at once, and "everywhere" was a lot closer together at the time. The expansion is that everywhere is becoming more distant from everywhere else, not that things are hurtling away from some central point.

Okay, let’s imagine the universe is like a big, big balloon that keeps getting bigger and bigger. 

A long time ago, everything was squished together in one tiny spot—like a dot on the balloon. Then, the balloon started to grow, and everything spread out.

Now, if you draw a tiny dot on a small balloon and then blow it up, that dot gets farther and farther away from you, but it also moves away from every other spot on the balloon. So, if you look in any direction on the balloon, you can see things that were close to the dot a long time ago—they’re all over the balloon now, not just in one spot.

That’s what happened with the galaxies in the universe. When the universe was tiny, all the galaxies were close together. But as the universe grew, the galaxies moved apart, and now they’re everywhere, like dots all over a big balloon. That’s why we see galaxies in every direction—they all started together and then spread out as the universe got bigger.
